Empirical Research Plan  
“Do More-Selective Colleges Causally Raise Earnings?  Evidence from the 1976 College & Beyond Cohort”

----------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) using quasi-random
variation in the set of admission offers a student receives.

Rationale  
• Each applicant faces many independent admission committees.  
• Conditional on the *observable* information in the application
(SAT, high-school rank, parental income, etc.), whether a given
committee says “yes” or “no” depends on idiosyncratic, unobserved
factors (essay readers, interviewer match, alumni legacy, slot
availability, etc.).  
• Among students who apply to both a highly-selective and a
less-selective college, being *admitted* to the more-selective
school creates exogenous (or at least plausibly exogenous) variation in
where the student actually enrolls.  
• This admission-offer variation has been used in other settings
(“multiple cut-offs,” “Bartik-type college choice,” “oracle
offers”); here it is a natural IV because (i) it strongly predicts the
selectivity of the school eventually attended, and (ii) conditional on
observables, the admissions decision of one school should not affect
earnings except through the college chosen.  

Formally, let  

  Z₁ᵢ = 1{student i is admitted to any college in the top quartile
             of the C&B selectivity distribution}  
  Z₂ᵢ = (net-tuition difference between the most-selective admission
             offer and the least-selective offer)  

Serve as instruments for  

  Tᵢ  = average SAT of classmates at the college *attended*.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: Peer selectivity of the college attended measured by the
freshman-class mean SAT score (or, in robustness checks, a dummy for
“top-quartile college”).  
• We will also estimate heterogeneous effects by the student’s family
background (parental income quartile, parental education, race).

Control/counterfactual  
• Students who attend less-selective colleges because they were
either not admitted to, or did not choose to attend, a
higher-selectivity option.  
• Because assignment is through an instrument, the “as-good-as-random”
comparison is between students *with the same application set* who
differ only in the admission-offer vector and, consequently, in the
school they choose.

Timing  
• Treatment occurs once—the freshman enrollment decision for the fall
of 1976. Outcomes are measured in 1995.  No staggered timing, so DID /
event-study frameworks are unnecessary.

----------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance: Being admitted to a selective college and/or
getting a favorable net-tuition gap must *predict* attending a more
selective institution.  
 Plausible: historical yield rates show a large first-stage.

A2. Instrument exogeneity (exclusion + independence): Conditional on
observable credentials and the list of schools applied to, the random
component of each college’s admission decision is unrelated to
unobserved earnings determinants.  
 Plausible but testable: will probe by adding rich controls, high-school
fixed effects, and application-set fixed effects.

A3. Exclusion restriction: Admission offers affect earnings *only*
through the selectivity and other observable characteristics of the
college actually attended (no direct channel).  
 Plausible: an unused offer per se should not raise wages 20 years
later except via college choice.

A4. Monotonicity: Nobody would *attend a *less* selective college* when
receiving an additional *highly* selective admission offer if all else
is equal (i.e., no defiers).  
 Reasonable: very few students turn down Harvard for a lower-ranked
school purely because it replied “yes,” though aid packages may
matter—hence the *net-price* instrument to help insure monotonicity.

A5. SUTVA: One student’s admission outcome does not affect another’s
earnings except through their own college choice.  
 Reasonable in a national sample.

----------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigations
----------------------------------------------------
T1. Omitted ability correlated with admissions outcomes.  
 Fix: control for a rich vector of academic credentials; include the
mean selectivity of *all* schools applied to (proxy for ambition and
ability); add high-school fixed effects.

T2. Financial-aid induced sorting (aid is correlated both with
admissions and family resources that influence later earnings).  
 Fix: include *net* tuition and its square in the control set; use aid
information as an *additional* instrument to separate price from
selectivity.

T3. Selective non-response in the 1995 earnings follow-up.  
 Fix: construct survey-response weights based on baseline covariates
and admissions outcomes; verify robustness by bounding (Lee bounds) on
attrition.

----------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------
```r
#############################################
# 0.  Packages
#############################################
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # OLS & IV regressions
library(ivreg)        # alternative IV
library(survey)       # weights
#############################################
# 1.  Load and merge data
#############################################
cb      <- fread("college_beyond_1976.csv")    # student-level
offers  <- fread("admission_offers.csv")       # one row per offer
costs   <- fread("net_price_offers.csv")       # aid information
inst    <- fread("institution_characteristics.csv")  # avg SAT, etc.

# merge institution characteristics onto offers
offers  <- merge(offers, inst, by = "college_id")

# collapse offers to student-level instruments
offers_student <- offers[ ,
   .(admit_to_selective = any(avg_sat >= quantile(inst$avg_sat, .75)),
     max_selectivity    = max(avg_sat * admit),
     min_selectivity    = min(avg_sat * admit + 999 * (1 - admit)),
     net_price_high_sel = min(net_price[avg_sat >= quantile(inst$avg_sat,.75)], na.rm=TRUE),
     net_price_low_sel  = min(net_price[avg_sat <  quantile(inst$avg_sat,.75)], na.rm=TRUE)
     ),
   by = student_id]

cb <- merge(cb, offers_student, by = "student_id")

#############################################
# 2.  Construct analysis variables
#############################################
cb[ , treat_selectivity := inst_avg_sat_attended ]     # continuous treatment
cb[ , high_selective    := as.integer(inst_avg_sat_attended >= 
                       quantile(inst$avg_sat, .75)) ] # binary robustness

# family background dummies
cb[ , low_income  := as.integer(parent_income_quartile == 1) ]
cb[ , high_income := as.integer(parent_income_quartile == 4) ]

# instrument(s)
cb[ , z1 := as.integer(admit_to_selective) ]
cb[ , z2 := net_price_low_sel - net_price_high_sel ]  # tuition gap

#############################################
# 3.  Main 2SLS specification
#############################################
# weights for non-response
des <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = cb, weights = ~followup_weight)

iv_main <- feols(log(earnings_1995) ~ treat_selectivity + 
                 hs_rank + sat_score + gpa_hs + 
                 factor(parent_income_quartile) + 
                 factor(race) + factor(sex) + 
                 factor(high_school_id) |
                 . ~ z1 + z2, 
                 data = des$variables, weights = des$variables$followup_weight)

summary(iv_main, cluster = "high_school_id")

#############################################
# 4.  Heterogeneity by family background
#############################################
iv_fb <- feols(log(earnings_1995) ~ treat_selectivity*low_income + 
               hs_rank + sat_score + gpa_hs |
               . ~ (z1 + z2)*low_income,
               data = des$variables,
               weights = des$variables$followup_weight)
summary(iv_fb, cluster = "high_school_id")

#############################################
# 5.  Robustness:  (i) OLS with rich controls, 
#                   (ii) replicate on NLS-72
#############################################
ols_rich <- feols(log(earnings_1995) ~ treat_selectivity + 
                  hs_rank + sat_score + gpa_hs +
                  factor(college_major) + 
                  factor(high_school_id),
                  data = cb, weights = ~followup_weight)
summary(ols_rich, cluster = "high_school_id")

# -- analogous code would load nls72.csv and re-estimate here --
```

----------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------
Prior: A one-standard-deviation increase in peer SAT (≈75 points in
this sample) should raise *annual* earnings by roughly 4–6 percent
(log-points) 20 years later, reflecting both human-capital and network
effects.  
Heterogeneity: The point estimate is likely *larger* for students from
low-income families (who gain more from networks) and smaller or even
zero for high-income students whose background already provides
comparable advantages.

----------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
----------------------------------------------------
C1 (Instrument relevance) ………………… 1  
C2 (Exclusion restriction) ………………… 0.5  
C3 (Independence / unconfoundedness) …… 0.5  
C4 (Monotonicity) …………………………… 0.8  
C5 (SUTVA) ……………………………………… 1  

Total ≈ 3.8 / 5 → “moderately credible but still requires sensitivity
analyses.”

----------------------------------------------------
End of plan
